explanations.explanation: Yes, the family leaves Bethlehem and goes to live in the land of Moab. The verse says the man from Bethlehem in Judah goes to reside in Moab with his wife and two sons (Ruth 1:1). Hunger in one place pushes them to start over in another. That move is what sets the whole story in motion.

Egypt is a place God’s people went during other hard times, but not in this story. Ruth 1:1 says they go to the land of Moab, not Egypt. Keeping those details sharp helps you track where God is working. Here, the story’s road runs through Moab.

Edom was a neighbor country, but it is not where this family goes. Ruth 1:1 says the man from Bethlehem in Judah goes to reside in the land of Moab. The writer wants us to notice Moab in particular. That’s where Naomi’s losses and Ruth’s choices will unfold.

That is right. Naomi’s sons marry two Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth (Ruth 1:4). Ruth starts here as a daughter-in-law from another land. Before long, she will be at the very center of what God is doing in this book.

Rachel is a well-known woman in Genesis, but she is not in this story. Ruth 1:4 names the two Moabite wives as Orpah and Ruth. Those are the names to keep in your hands here. Ruth is the one who will walk all the way to Bethlehem with Naomi.

Dinah appears in Genesis, but she is not part of Naomi’s family. In Ruth 1:4, Naomi’s sons marry Moabite women named Orpah and Ruth. The writer is pointing us to Ruth’s name on purpose. She will be key to Naomi’s future and to God’s plan.

Yes. After about ten years in Moab, both Mahlon and Chilion die, and Naomi is left without her two sons and without her husband (Ruth 1:5). It is layer on layer of loss for her. That is the weight she is carrying when she hears news from Bethlehem.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: The passage does not mention a house burning. Ruth 1:5 tells us the tragedy is that both of Naomi’s sons die, leaving her without husband and sons. The focus is on people lost, not things lost. That deep sorrow shapes every choice she makes next.

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: Naomi’s body is not what the text talks about here. Ruth 1:5 says both of her sons die, and she is left without them and without her husband. The pain is in losing her family. That is what makes her feel so empty when she finally goes back home.

Yes. Naomi hears in Moab that the LORD has attended to His people by providing them with food (Ruth 1:6). The famine that once pushed her out is easing. That mercy from God is what turns her feet back toward Bethlehem.

A king will come into Israel’s story later, but Ruth 1:6 is not about that. Naomi hears that the LORD has visited His people by giving them food. In a famine, full tables are the good news. That provision is what pulls Naomi homeward.

The verse does not mention a battle win. Ruth 1:6 says the LORD has attended to His people by providing them with food. When hunger has been the problem, bread on the table is the victory. That is the news Naomi moves on.

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: That is it. Out on the road, Naomi tells Orpah and Ruth to go back, each of them to her mother’s home (Ruth 1:8). She loves them enough to release them. She even asks the LORD to show them loving devotion as they have shown to her.

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: Naomi is not giving travel tips. She is giving them an open door. Ruth 1:8 says she tells each of them to go back to her mother’s home, and she blesses them in the LORD’s name. Her words are about their future, not the pace of the journey.

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: They are walking with her, but Naomi is not saying they must stay. In Ruth 1:8 she actually tells them to go back to their mothers’ homes. She is trying to free them from the hard road she is on. That makes their response even more powerful.

Yes. Naomi blesses them by saying the LORD would enable each of them to find rest in the home of her new husband (Ruth 1:9). She wants them to have stability and care again. Even in her grief, she is praying for their good.

Naomi really does talk about new husbands here. Ruth 1:9 says she prays the LORD will grant that each of them finds rest in the home of her new husband. That is her picture of a settled, safe future for them. Her blessing looks forward, even while her own story feels broken.

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: Exactly. After the weeping and the kiss, both Orpah and Ruth say they will return with Naomi to her people (Ruth 1:10). At this point, their hearts are set on staying with her. The real test of that promise is still coming.

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: They actually say the opposite. Ruth 1:10 says they tell Naomi they will return with her to her people. They are not planning to wait back in Moab. Their first answer is full commitment to Naomi’s road.

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Visits are not what they offer. Ruth 1:10 shows them saying they will return with Naomi to her people. That is a promise to move, not just to stop by. Only later will we see who keeps going with her.

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: Yes. Naomi says even if she could have a husband that very night and then have sons, she asks, would they wait for those boys to grow up (Ruth 1:12-13). She is showing how unrealistic that path would be. She is trying to talk them out of tying their future to her emptiness.

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: Naomi is not asking them to raise children. She is asking if they would wait for sons to grow up to be husbands. Ruth 1:12-13 has her saying that even if she could have sons immediately, it would not make sense for Orpah and Ruth to wait for them. Her point is that they need real, near-term hope.

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: She does not suggest they go ahead of her. Naomi is pressing on the idea of waiting for sons who do not exist yet. In Ruth 1:12-13 she asks if they would wait for sons to grow up and stay from having husbands. She is showing them how empty her own prospects are.

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: That matches her own words. Naomi says it is much more bitter for her than for them because the hand of the LORD has gone out against her (Ruth 1:13). That is how her losses feel from the inside. She is speaking out of deep hurt and confusion.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: The text does not say her own people have turned on her. In Ruth 1:13, Naomi says it is more bitter for her because the hand of the LORD has gone out against her. She is wrestling with what God has allowed in her life. That is where she feels the weight.

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: The passage never says the Moabites have attacked or rejected her. Naomi’s words in Ruth 1:13 point to something else. She says it is more bitter for her because the hand of the LORD has gone out against her. Her struggle is with what she believes God has done, not with a crowd around her.
Yes. Ruth 1:14 says Orpah kisses her mother-in-law goodbye. It is a real, tearful farewell. Then she turns back, while Ruth holds on.

The verse makes a point of telling us she does. Ruth 1:14 says Orpah kisses her mother-in-law goodbye and then leaves. That goodbye matters in the story. It shows she loved Naomi, even though she chose a different road than Ruth.

Ruth does not turn back with Orpah here. Ruth 1:14 says Orpah kisses Naomi goodbye, but Ruth clings to her. The story highlights Ruth staying right beside Naomi. That choice will shape everything that comes next.
Correct. Ruth does not go home with Orpah. Ruth 1:14 says Orpah kisses Naomi goodbye, but Ruth clings to her. Ruth’s grip on Naomi is her first loud action of loyalty in this journey.

Yes. After Orpah turns back, Naomi tells Ruth to follow her sister-in-law back to her people and her gods (Ruth 1:15). Naomi is still trying to release Ruth from a hard future. She is not expecting the answer she is about to hear.

Naomi really does tell Ruth to follow Orpah back. Ruth 1:15 says, after Orpah goes back to her people and her gods, Naomi tells Ruth to follow her. Naomi keeps pushing Ruth toward an easier path. Ruth’s reply goes in a very different direction.

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: That is the heart of it. Ruth promises that Naomi’s people will be her people and Naomi’s God will be her God (Ruth 1:16). She is not just moving towns. She is binding herself to Naomi’s community and to the LORD Himself.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: Ruth’s promise runs deeper than house chores. In Ruth 1:16 she says Naomi’s people will be her people and Naomi’s God will be her God. She is stepping into Naomi’s whole life and faith. The verse does not focus on a building at all.

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: Ruth will learn plenty, but that is not the wording of her promise. She says Naomi’s people will be her people and Naomi’s God will be her God (Ruth 1:16). That is a covenant kind of statement. It is about belonging and worship more than customs.
Yes. Ruth calls on the LORD and says that only death will separate her from Naomi (Ruth 1:17). She is staking her future on this promise. It is a strong, lifelong commitment, not a short-term plan.

Ruth does not leave herself that kind of escape hatch. In Ruth 1:17 she says may the LORD punish her if anything but death separates her and Naomi. She is saying not even distance should break this bond. Her loyalty is meant to last to the grave.

Ruth is not saying marriage would separate them. She calls the LORD to witness that only death will separate her from Naomi (Ruth 1:17). That is a powerful vow from a daughter-in-law. She is promising to stay, whatever changes come.

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: Yes. When Naomi sees that Ruth is determined to go with her, she stops speaking to her about turning back (Ruth 1:18). Ruth’s words settled the question. From here on, they walk the road together.

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: By this point, Naomi has tried, and Ruth has stood firm. Ruth 1:18 says when Naomi sees Ruth is determined to go with her, she stops trying to persuade her. She does not send her back again. She lets Ruth’s commitment stand.

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: Naomi no longer pushes Ruth away once she hears that vow. Ruth 1:18 says she sees Ruth is determined to go with her and stops speaking to her about it. There is no order to stay in Moab. The two widows move forward together.

That is right. When Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem, the whole town is stirred, and the women say, can this be Naomi (Ruth 1:19). Time and sorrow have changed her. Their question shows both recognition and surprise.

The women may have wondered many things, but the text gives us one line. Ruth 1:19 says they ask, can this be Naomi. The focus is on her, not on her missing husband by name. Her very appearance tells a story.

They do not treat her like a stranger. Ruth 1:19 says they are stirred and ask, can this be Naomi. They recognize her, even through all the change. That question opens the door for Naomi to speak her heart.

Yes. Naomi tells the women of Bethlehem to call her Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with her (Ruth 1:20). The new name matches how her life feels to her. She is carrying grief that has soaked down deep.

Hannah is another woman of faith in Scripture, but she is not Naomi’s new name. In Ruth 1:20, Naomi tells the women to call her Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with her. She is choosing a name that fits her pain. The text keeps that connection tight.

Leah is a different woman in Genesis, not Naomi’s chosen name. Ruth 1:20 says Naomi tells them, call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me. Mara lines up with the bitterness she feels. That is the word she reaches for in this moment.

That statement does not match what Naomi says. In Ruth 1:21 she tells them she went away full, but the LORD has brought her back empty. She feels like she left with a full life and has returned with her arms bare. Her words are a window into her grief.

Correct. Naomi does not say she went away empty and came back full. Ruth 1:21 has her saying, I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. That is how her losses look to her. The story will show us more of what God is doing behind that feeling.

Yes. Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest (Ruth 1:22). That detail matters, because harvest time will open doors for them. God is already lining up provision in the background.

The writer points to a different crop here. Ruth 1:22 says they come to Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest. That timing is not just scenery. It sets up how Ruth will find work and favor in the next part of the story.

The harvest in view is grain, not olives. Ruth 1:22 says they arrive at Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest. That is when the fields are busy and full. Out in those fields, God will start answering needs Naomi can barely put into words yet.
